Divisive climate change satire Digger is set to lose $250 million by the end of its run, according to TheWrap. TheWrap claims insiders at new Warner Bros. overlords Skydance are not anticipating Digger will exceed a worldwide box office total of $40 million following its alarming opening weekend results (just $8 million in US domestic takings and a further $12 million in international receipts).
Warner Bros. has not commented on the claims. Warner Bros., which is being acquired by Paramount in a controversial $110 billion deal, will now exist alongside the latter under parent company Skydance.
Directed by back-to-back Best Director Oscar winner Alejandro G. Iñárritu (Birdman, The Revenant) and starring screen legend Tom Cruise, Digger has split both critics and audiences. Attempts have been made to weaponise the mixed reaction to its favour, but it doesn’t appear to have translated to increased interest in the film at the box office. IGN’s review notes Digger has “the budget to let some very talented artists work at the top of their game” but stresses it’s “far from a must-watch.”

item.title: Jeremy Grows a Car: A Clarkson’s Farm Special will air on Prime in 2027.
item.description:
Prime Video has confirmed a new, one-off episode of its Clarkson’s Farm series, which will see host Jeremy Clarkson temporarily return to his Top Gear and The Grand Tour roots for an automotive-themed special.
Jeremy Grows a Car: A Clarkson’s Farm Special will see Clarkson attempt what Prime proposes is a world first: he will grow and build his own car from produce sourced from his personal farm, Diddly Squat.
Using the Jaguar F-Type V6S as his base, Clarkson will be restoring it using his own Diddly leather interior and wool carpets, and will also be attempting to grow a crop of flax fiber to turn into a sustainable flax-composite material – an alternative to carbon fiber Prime claims is already on the radar of major car makers.
Clarkson will be aided in his car-building quest by legendary car designer Ian Callum CBE. Callum is the designer of the original Jaguar F-Type, as well as the Jaguar XK and C-X75, plus the Aston Martin Vanquish, DB7, and DB9. He was also involved with the Ford RS200 and the Nissan R390.
Jeremy Grows a Car: A Clarkson’s Farm Special will air in 2027.

item.title: Developer Fuse Games aims to release an update to increase party size from three to six players “within the first few weeks of launch.”
item.description:
Star Wars: Galactic Racer has broadly proven to be a smash hit with critics, and fans seem similarly enthusiastic, but developer Fuse Games has heard the concern regarding multiplayer party sizes and has responded via the game’s official social media. Resultingly, it appears we should be able to expect an update to increase the multiplayer party size from three to six players at some point within the next few weeks.
“Thank you so much for your feedback and we’d like to let you and everyone on this thread know that we hear you,” the developer responded to various fans raising the concern online. “We’re working on an update to increase the party size from three to six players, with the aim of releasing it within the first few weeks of launch.”
More details will be available soon, the developer noted.
IGN’s Star Wars: Galactic Racer review called it “a fabulous looking and frantically fast anti-grav racer… that has successfully lit the afterburners on a long-dormant slice of the Star Wars universe.”

item.title: Mixtape developer Beethoven & Dinosaur has won a trifecta of awards at the 2026 AGDAs, including Excellence in Visual Art, Excellence in Sound Design, and Game of the Year.
item.description:
Melbourne-based studio Beethoven & Dinosaur has won Game of the Year for its music-themed, minigame-driven adventure game Mixtape at the 2026 Australian Game Developer Awards (AGDAs). Mixtape also won Excellence in Visual Art and Excellence in Sound Design.
“Mixtape was the outcome of an amazingly talented team,” said Beethoven & Dinosaur director Johnny Galvatron. “To go from wanting to make a game around Devo to creating something that resonates with so many people is mind blowing. We’re lucky to be part of such a talented community, and I’m so proud of Mixtape and my team.”
Praise for Mixtape from the AGDA’s judges noted that “[it] is a triumph in virtual storytelling, pairing a distinct visual identity with heartfelt music to deliver one of the most memorable experiences in recent memory.”
IGN’s May review of Mixtape called it a “musical delight from start to finish” and declared it “sets a new standard for coming-of-age stories in video games and does so with a masterful sense of style.” Its soundtrack includes cuts from Devo, The Smashing Pumpkins, Silverchair, Iggy Pop, and many other acts.
Other winners from this year’s AGDAs include rhythm game Bits & Bops from Tempo Lab Games for both Excellence in Gameplay and Excellence in Accessibility, and puzzle platformer Schrodinger’s Cat Burglar from Abandoned Sheep for Excellence in Narrative. The Studio of the Year was awarded to Canberra-based Uppercut Games.
The AGDAs, which have been hosted in various forms since 2002, are presented by Australia’s Interactive Games and Entertainment Association. These days it forms part of Melbourne International Games Week, which is culminating this weekend with PAX Aus 2026.

item.title: Bit Reactor, the developer of Star Wars Zero Company, has begun returning some of its staff to the team after furloughing an estimated 80% of employees just before the game’s launch.
item.description:
Bit Reactor, the developer of Star Wars Zero Company, has begun returning some of its staff to the team after furloughing an estimated 80% of employees just before the game’s launch.
Bit Reactor’s CEO Greg Foertsch revealed the news in a public post on October 7, where he explained that the furloughs were necessary to “help us eventually bring as many people back as possible.”
Foertsh said that bringing these staff members back to Bit Reactor was an “important step forward” in the studio’s “continued support for Zero Company,” and that the team looks forward to sharing more updates about the game “soon.”
“Having to ask team members to step away after we navigated unexpected business developments outside of our control and so close to launch was an incredibly difficult decision,” Foertsh wrote. “...This team means a tremendous amount to me, and I am incredibly proud of what we have accomplished together. Thank you to our fans for the incredible response to the game and for supporting us along this journey.”
Sources with information about the situation told GameFile that the number of Bit Reactor’s payrolled staff now account for “more than half of what it had been ahead of the furloughs,” meaning that there is still a sizeable chunk of furloughed staff who aren’t getting paid.
Star Wars Zero Company launched in August 2026 to rave reviews, getting a sparkling nine out of 10 from our reviewers here at IGN who praised it for being an “excellent tactical game that does a fantastic job of slathering on the same cinematic look and feel we saw in Respawn's Star Wars Jedi games, incorporating strong characters and a storyline that's refreshingly centered on non-Force users and a non-traditional villain.”
Despite its success, much of Bit Reactor’s staff were placed on leave without pay just before Zero Company launched, with reports indicating around 80% of employees were affected. This has become a recurring trend within the game development industry, to the point where Gears of War: E-Day developers were overcome with worry that they would get laid off after “crunching hard” to get the game out on time.
This is the latest news to get revealed about Zero Company after GameFile uncovered legal documents revealing that the game was initially pitched as a title within the Titanfall universe, with specific connections to Apex Legends. While this pitch ultimately didn’t go through, it’s certainly intriguing enough to make us wonder what such a game would have looked like, had it actually been made.

item.title: Samuel L. Jackson has confirmed that we won’t be seeing Nick Fury in Avengers: Doomsday, but said that his character is set to return in Avengers: Secret Wars.
item.description:
Samuel L. Jackson has confirmed that we won’t be seeing Nick Fury in Avengers: Doomsday, but said that his character is set to return in Avengers: Secret Wars.
Jackson revealed this information in a red carpet interview with The Direct ahead of the premier for The Beast, his newest film. After The Direct’s interviewer noted that Nick Fury hasn’t been spotted in a Marvel movie for some time, Jackson said that he will be in the next film after Doomsday — which, according to the current slate laid out by Marvel Studios, is Avengers: Secret Wars.
He didn’t elaborate on what we can expect from Fury’s appearance in this movie, saying that Marvel only told him that he’d be in it and nothing more.
"Next movie... [The] movie after this one,” he told the outlet. “I have no idea. [Marvel] hasn't told me anything, other than, 'You're not gonna be in this movie. You'll be in the next.'"
Thus far, Marvel has been keeping the cast of Secret Wars close to its chest; in September, Noah Jupe was added to the roster of actors set to star in the film in an as-yet unrevealed role. Anthony Mackie has also been confirmed for the movie, but says he won’t be able start filming until his run in a broadway showing of Macbeth ends in July 2027.
Secret Wars recently ran into some significant roadblocks, with multiple insiders claiming that filming for the project has been delayed until early 2027, most likely in January. Thus far, no reason for this delay has been revealed, but it’s enough to spark anxiety among fans — many of whom feel that Doomsday needs to be a home run of a movie to keep interest in the current MCU saga.
Secret Wars is set to cap off the Russo brothers’ involvement with the MCU, with the two saying in June 2026 that they won’t be directing a third film to create a new Avengers trilogy. The movie marks the sixth major cross-over event in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, and will serve as the final chapter in the Multiverse saga, putting an end to the innumerable variations of characters that have been popping up in Marvel’s TV series and films over the MCU’s last three phases.
Recent reporting indicates that the Battleworld will be involved somehow, given that it serves as the setting for the Secret Wars comic storyline, though this hasn’t been confirmed. It would be a fitting way for the Multiverse Saga to end, though, as Battleworld is a patchwork planet made up of several different versions of Earth combined by none other than Dr Doom.
For now, we’ll just have to wait and see what’s in store, and if Avengers: Doomsday lives up to the hype. The movie releases in theaters on December 18, 2026.

item.title: The developers of Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse are wearing their love of fighting games on their sleeves, as eagle-eyed fans have spotted some unmistakable references to classic fighting game characters in its demo.
item.description:
The developers of Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse are wearing their love of fighting games on their sleeves, as eagle-eyed fans have spotted some unmistakable references to classic fighting game characters in its demo.
Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse released a free demo on October 1, 2026, giving players a brief taste of what the game’s combat will look like. In this game, we take control of Rose Belmont, who navigates the ruined streets of 1500s Paris with a sword and her mother’s magical tarot cards.
If the demo is anything to go by, this game will be a treat for hardcore Metroidvania fans, as it includes a wealth of secret areas to uncover. One of these areas can be accessed in the demo, which gives you a pair of brass knuckle-style MMA gloves called Cestus. The weapon stacks on damage to enemies the more you hit them, encouraging players to go on the offensive.
After Rose finishes an attack using Cestus, she will strike a pose for a few seconds. These poses cycle seemingly at random, but they’re clearly intentional, and each boasts a unique animation. It didn’t take long for players to notice some striking similarities between these poses and the fighting stances of classic fighting game characters, of which there are a good handful.
Twitter/X user and Castlevania fan StockeTepes compiled these poses in a video, showing Rose settling into the idle poses for Ryu, Chun-Li, Oro, and Sagat, as well as Mai Shiranui and Akuma / Oni. Even Spider-Man’s iconic pose from Marvel vs Capcom 2 was included. Other fans pointed out that Rose’s air-to-air combo using Cestus mimics that of Akuma’s in-air fireball attack, Zanku Hadouken (or, in my opinion, M. Bison's Hell Attack).
Castlevania is a franchise known for tipping its hat to fighting games; if you’ve played Symphony of the Night, you’ll know that the inputs for Alucard’s purchasable spells read exactly like the motions for special moves in a fighting game, and the gauntlet-style weapon Fist of Tulkas basically let you throw out a Hadouken. And in Portrait of Ruin, players can unlock Martial Arts moves that give you special abilities, which require special fighting game-style inputs to pull off. Konami even released a Castlevania fighting game in 2008 called Castlevania Judgment (though whether or not it's remembered fondly is a matter of personal opinion).
I told you, Castlevania LOVES fighting games 🔥 And the tradition of calling back to them continues with Belmont's Curse! So I made a lil edit showcasing how the Demo's secret weapon, Cestus, homages idle poses for many of it's iconic characters.MUCH more coming stay tuned 😈 https://t.co/7UVd7OFSTQ
Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse officially releases on October 15. In the meantime, there’s no shortage of Castlevania games for you to play as you wait for the latest entry in the series to launch. (My personal favorites are Symphony of the Night, Super Castlevania IV, and the OG Castlevania game — but there’s literally more than 30 to choose from!)
That’s not all; the iconic soundtrack of the Castlevania franchise is getting its own live power rock-symphony in March 2026, with showings in London, Tokyo, and Los Angeles. It’s a great time to be a Castlevania fan — but a terrible night to have a curse.

item.title: We got the chance to sit down with the one and only Guillermo del Toro as part of our IGN30 Icons Series, where he let us in on his favorite games, how he made his iconic movies, and his experience working with some of the biggest stars in filmmaking.
item.description:
We got the chance to sit down with the one and only Guillermo del Toro as part of our IGN30 Icons Series, where he let us in on his favorite games, how he made his iconic movies, and his experience working with some of the biggest stars in filmmaking.
He also chatted about Pan’s Labyrinth, which is turning 20 years old this year. To celebrate, it’s coming back to theaters this weekend — but if you’d like some extra context before you sit down to see it again, check out our conversation with del Toro, who told us about the inspiration behind the Pale Man and how he stretched the movie’s budget to create some of its massive set pieces.
We’ve transcribed the interview in full below, where del Toro explained what it was like working with Wesley Snipes on Blade 2 and how he almost made a BioShock movie.
Brian Altano (IGN): From Kronos to The Shape of Water to Frankenstein, it is an honor to be talking to the maestro of movie monsters, Mr. Guillermo Del Toro. It's very nice to meet you. Thank you for coming. This is the 20th anniversary of Pan's Labyrinth, which makes me feel old. I don't know how you feel about it.
Guillermo del Toro: Older.
Brian Altano (IGN): So, you have been making crazy monsters in beautiful worlds for the longest time. You started off inspired by things like Universal’s monsters, [like the] Creature from the Black Lagoon. What is it about that era that spoke to you then, and continues to resonate with you now?
Guillermo del Toro: I think I was a monster kid, which means that the creatures are important in the storytelling of these fairytales, because I think they're fables or parables or fairytales. And it has to be creature-centric for me to be attracted to it. Everybody says, "Oh, don't show the creature." I think, show it, please. I'm seven years old. I want to see it. I want to love it. I want to see how well designed it is. I want to discover the whole world that comes in with the creature design. Creature design ushers a different reality. So those are important. When Milicent Patrick — who designed the Gill-man for Creature from the Black Lagoon — designed the Metaluna Mutant on Island Earth, when they gave her an opportunity, it came from outer space. She designed the creature. She has a signature, and I can see what her design signature is. And as a kid, it's like meeting a movie star. You say, "Oh, this was Jack Pierce designing this creature. This was Dick Smith. This was the Wesmers. This was all the makeup heroes of mine."
Brian Altano (IGN): So when you saw the sort of less tangible horror, which it's like a fog or a mist or something like that, you're like, "That's cool, but I want a monster.”
Guillermo del Toro: Well, that's what I want to make. That doesn't define what I want to watch. I want to watch everything that is good. But as a filmmaker, up until Frankenstein, I'm very creature-centric. I think that has changed now. I don't know what I am or where I'm going. I have sort of a new horizon, but Frankenstein was a culmination of my creature-centric period, which is, by the way, where is it rooted at? Little Red Ridinghood. You need the wolf. The wolf is the creature in that. And you need something that embodies a concept. Good, evil, purity, tragedy. The Creature in Frankenstein is a tragic humanity. Pan is a trickster. The Pale Man is a blind veracity. It's not just that they are cool-looking. It's that they embody the conceptual part of the tale. They actually mean something tangible. Godzilla is absolutely a first large-scale God, the power of nature, the tragedy of atomic energy. It's a concept made flesh.
Brian Altano (IGN): It's not just this wrecking ball that comes in. There's a pain behind it.
Guillermo del Toro: There is the tragic undertones of the design of Godzilla, the fact that they wanted the skin of Godzilla to look like the after effect of a nuclear blast victim. I mean, there is thought on that — the fact that he was this sort of grayish-brown in the original. There is a lot of thought. Jack Pierce designing the Grizzly on Frankenstein — he wanted to sort of retrofit the history of the autopsic work that put it together. The scars, the opening of the skull in a sort of weird, can-of-tomatoes way.
Brian Altano (IGN): You like to get your hands dirty. You like to build stuff. You make model kits. Your Cabinet of Curiosity is a very tangible thing. It feels like a lot of filmmakers are sort of moving around
or away from that, but that is something that feels so core to your philosophy of filmmaking.
Guillermo del Toro: Yeah. Each filmmaker is like, I see Chris Nolan completely going to battle for negative and he's entrenched there. I see Jim Cameron exploring beyond capture. He's actually melding actors’ performances with how it translates into digital. Each filmmaker is on a quest, I think. And my quest is handmade by humans for humans.
Brian Altano (IGN): I love that. Christopher Nolan mentioned that you were a big inspiration for a lot of his practical effects in the Odyssey, specifically the Cyclops.
Guillermo del Toro: Cyclops, yeah.
Brian Altano (IGN): Did you see it?
Guillermo del Toro: Yeah, yeah. No, I saw it with him.
Brian Altano (IGN): Oh my God, that's awesome.
Guillermo del Toro: He said, "I want to show you the movie." And we saw it in IMAX. We talked after, we talked before. I mean, I think he's just — there is such a signature and such a vision. I mean, the word visionary is thrown around a little too much, but I think Chris has always been. I've known him now fortunately for about 15 years or more. And he's always been absolutely laser-focused.
Brian Altano (IGN): Did you like what he did with the cyclops?
Guillermo del Toro: Yeah, I loved it.
Brian Altano (IGN): Me too.
Guillermo del Toro: Loved it. I mean, I love everything. I asked him, “So when Matt Damon is in the tempestuous waters, how did you do it?” He's like, "We put him in the water on a tempestuous day." It was so fantastic to hear him answer that. And I remember when I talked to him about his philosophy of sound mixing, because I asked him that back in the days of Interstellar, and he said, "To me, dialogue is part of the score. It's not so much what they say, but the rhythm of how they say it and the intention." And I thought that was… Now and then, when I mix, now and then I go, "It's a rhythmic thing."
Brian Altano (IGN): You worked on Mimic, which, for me, that was sort of like a Creature from the Black Lagoon for me. It's funny to say, right? Because when I was a kid and I did the same thing, I was going —
Guillermo del Toro: It's a monster movie.
Brian Altano (IGN): I was like, "I want to watch a monster movie." And I saw that one and the setting. I had grown up going to the Museum of Natural History in New York City.
Guillermo del Toro: Yeah. Well, that's where we went!
Brian Altano (IGN): And it actually changed that museum for me for a while, because I would go there and I'd be like, "Are we good?" All the rooms were a little dark.
Guillermo del Toro: Yeah, of course. The Natural History Museum in New York, to me, is Disneyland. It's a portal to imagination. And the exhibits are so exquisitely crafted. They are one of the places that have inspired me the most.
Brian Altano (IGN): I could spend hours looking up at that whale up there. The way that movie came together was sort of out of your hands. There were a lot of people kind of hacking it apart. Was there any time during that where you're like, "I don't want to do this anymore. This process is so..."
Guillermo del Toro: To a point. It's too early to quit when you're 33. That's true. You don't want to quit, but I wanted to quit that way of making movies. I was very careful to try to regain independence with Devil's Wagon supported by Pedro Almodovar. I was lucky enough that he liked what I did. And I made it a point. I was being pushed to do Blade 2 first. I said, "I'm doing Devil's Wagon first. I'm not going to go back to an industrial movie making environment until I cleanse my soul." And I made it a point. Many times people say, "Oh, I would never sell out." Well, you don't know until someone's buying. And I can tell you 100% sure of the many defects I have. I've never sold out.
Brian Altano (IGN): I believe it. I believe it. Do you think that you had to go through what you did with Mimic before you did Blade 2 and Hellboy?
Guillermo del Toro: Yes, because it makes a difference. I said, “Okay, so when I do Blade 2, I'm not going to try to fashion an auteurial [film].” I'm going to just go and say, “Okay, can I give you a six pack pizza, vox, balls-to-the-wall, fun, almost like a musical, and have it ooze atmosphere and coolness. And then you don't have to worry about anything else. Still, there's streaks of Frankenstein on it.
Brian Altano (IGN): Again, you've mentioned before the thing about sort of filmmakers making one movie. Can you explain that philosophy a bit?
Guillermo del Toro: It's actually, ‘One life fuels a movie.’ I would argue that the range would be between Devil's Wagon and Pacific Rim. That's the range of the modulation of the thing. But at the end of the day, you have a style, you have a signature. And I find it amazing with, for example, Alfonso Cuarón. You can do Gravity or you can do Roma. You would say it's not the same movie, but it is. Because I know what Alfonso's looking for, which is the connection with reality of the earth, almost like a transcendental approach. Gravity. I remember I was in the middle of the post-production, the studio didn't believe in the movie, and they wanted Alfonso to put helicopters coming to the rescue of Sandra Bullock at the end. I said, "No." He said, "Well, what about the sound of helicopters?" "No.” "What about the radio saying, ‘We're coming for you?’” I said, "No.” He said, "The only thing that she's recuperating is her footing on earth. That's what the movie's about.” Because it grounds it. It's an auteurial movie. So you have a voice and you use it for different songs, but it's the same voice.
Brian Altano (IGN): When you made Blade 2, you can just tell you had a ton of fun making that movie.
Guillermo del Toro: Actually, it's probably that and Pacific Rim are the two most fun movies I've ever shot. I really had fun. It may have been held by the fact that Red Bull had just come out and I didn't know how to use it. So I was drinking, and I'm not joking, about 40 Red Bulls a day.
Brian Altano (IGN): Man,that is amazing.
Guillermo del Toro: I was like in a cocaine movie. I was like, come on, let's go. And I would order cases and cases of Red Bull and throw them to the extras.
Brian Altano (IGN): I want to change the IGN review scale now. Instead of one to 10, I want to be like, “This is a 40 Red Bull movie.”
Guillermo del Toro: When I went back to America, Red Bull started traveling from Europe to there. And my doctor said, "You cannot consume more than four." I was drinking 40. The arterial damage, man.
Brian Altano (IGN): They announced a Blade reboot at Comic-Con years ago and they were never able to make it. And why do you think it's so difficult to get a movie like that done?
Guillermo del Toro: I'm telling you, and I mean it because I know it, 50% of the bladeness of Blade is Wesley Snipes.
Brian Altano (IGN): Wesley Snipes?
Guillermo del Toro: 100%. He is not the most linear actor to deal with, right?
Brian Altano (IGN): Right.
Guillermo del Toro: But every time he stood in front of the lens, I said, “That’s a movie star. That’s Blade.” Completely. For example, I showed him a gun we designed — beautiful, [Dieter] Reinhardt, Ron Pearlman ends up using it, with a blade on the front — and he looked at it. “Not for Blade. Cold gun, but not for Blade.” I said, “Why?” He said, “Because Blade is the weapon.” He said, “I don't want the toys. I want the man. The man is a dangerous guy. You give me too many toys, and that’s the Batmobile and the Bat belt. That's not Blade.” And I went, “Ah, this guy knows it.” And Every time [Snipes] landed, every time he turned, he’s a Neil Adams comic book [character]. And he has the natural sort of comic book [look]. I think Blade 1, Steve’s movie, changed the history of comic book movies for me, period. Because before that, you had either the cleanliness, the beauty, and sort of wholesomeness of Richard Donner's Superman, or you had the quirkiness of Tim Burton’s Batman. But this is what ushered the ‘tude, the edge. Without Steve Norrington's Blade, I don't think there is The Matrix. I don't think there is X-Men. I think what they did is monumental. And then I inherited and was completely, irresponsibly happy to do that.”
Brian Altano (IGN): So 50% of Blade is Wesley Snipes.
Guillermo del Toro: 100%. 100% is 50%.
Brian Altano (IGN): And the other 50% is Red Bull.
Guillermo del Toro: The other 50% is the filmmaker articulating. I mean, I had four or five moving boxes worth of dailies from [Stephen Norrington's] movie. And I studied all those VHS tapes. I understood exactly how he shot it. He did some formations that were really, extraordinarily weird. For example, he had a low camera with a longer lens in front of a high camera with a wide lens facing each other. His assistant called it — very impolitely and politically [incorrect] — they called it the Polish firing squad position. I didn't make that joke. I just repeated it. And then I started his formations and I said, “Okay, I'm going to go at it differently.” But there is one setup on Blade 2, which is 13 cameras working at the same time like a ballet. This camera is moving this way and then it crosses this one right on time for my cut. So I would cut before we shoot. So what they did is extraordinary. I know it.
Brian Altano (IGN): In your Blade 2 movie commentary, there's a sequence where you say, "This is my Dr. Manhattan shot." I love that so much. Obviously as a Watchman fan, a lot of directors sort of hide their influences.
Guillermo del Toro: I talk about them.
Brian Altano (IGN): Explain that, because obviously some people, I think they're sort of a little ashamed of jumping off of an idea that they may have seen before, that they might have inherited. But you've always been —
Guillermo del Toro: Because you're not rephrasing. When you take something and change it, it's a permutation. I mean, for example, the classical compositions are only so many. When you're doing a format, for example, you're doing a tango. It has to be a tango. It's on a certain tempo. When you're doing a waltz, there is a tempo. So you're taking a form and you're completely remixing it. Every chef in every restaurant, in every part of the world, whether it's a fast food service or… the hot cuisine of Michelin star restaurants, they're using the same ingredients. And you're not ashamed of pepper. You're not ashamed of a carrot, or what they call the mother sauce in France in the cooking — You have celery, carrot, onion. Ingredients are ingredients. And when I say, “This is my Dr. Manhattan shot,” well, I'm saying it's my Jack Kirby shot. Because that shot is very Jack Kirby. And then Jack Kirby, you have to talk to him to [see] where it comes from, but you are probably influenced by Milton Caniff. It's a lineage of storytellers. There is not such a thing as an ingredient you should not mention, because as we were discussing, I think for chefs coming up, it's important to disclose how you cook, how you bleach, how you blanch the potatoes. It's good to say this is what I did and it's very different.
Brian Altano (IGN): I appreciate that because I think that the making of stuff, the behind the scenes stuff, it is exactly the kind of thing that inspires new filmmakers.
Guillermo del Toro: Yes, 100%.
Brian Altano (IGN): And you made The Making of Frankenstein, which I watched immediately after Frankenstein. And it was fascinating to me, because I think coming from an era where you grew up looking at magazines of like, this is how they're making movies or watching the DVD actuals and Blu-rays and stuff like that, that's the stuff that people see and they go, "This isn't impossible anymore. This is something that I can start doing myself."
Guillermo del Toro: Yeah. I mean, as of lately, the last few releases on Blu-ray, I paid for the totality, or most of the behind the scenes content, because I wanted it to be in the disc. And I don't want it to be in the disc to sing our praises — I want it, because if you live in a part of the world or in an economic condition where you cannot afford film school, but your local library has the discs, you can learn how to make movies. If you come at it sincerely, it's not from the beginning. You want to talk about how hard it was and how you were thinking [about] this thing, but you went that way. So, I think they're very useful sort of substitutes for film school.
Brian Altano (IGN): Is there sort of like a scene in the movies you've made where every artist knows how difficult it is to translate the idea that's in your head to something that exists finally in real life, whether that's a drawing or a painting. It always filters and changes in some way. Is there a specific scene or collection of scenes that has come the closest from being like, "This is the idea in my mind. This is the scene in the film."
Guillermo del Toro: The Pale Man.
Brian Altano (IGN): Yeah?
Guillermo del Toro: The Pale Man in Pan’s Labyrinth. It changed a lot, but once the creature was set, once I found the creature in pre-production, I looked at a photo of a manta ray face up. And I saw the poster of Phantasm where the woman is screaming and you can see her eyes. And through many permutations, it ended up being that creature. But the moment I saw that creature, the scene was exactly what it is. And Pacific Rim, I knew exactly what I wanted to do to give the scale to the robots. I knew I wanted them in the rain. I knew I wanted them in what I call Goth-tech. And finally, I would say Frankenstein. But Frankenstein changed a lot when Jacob Elordi came in. So I mean, to some degree, those would be very close.
Brian Altano (IGN): Because at a certain point it is out of your hands, especially when it becomes part of an actor's experience.
Guillermo del Toro: It's never quite that simple. People think filmmaking is chess. It isn't. It's a contact sport. Or you're playing tennis. They serve, you return. Directing is knowing how to serve, but you also know how to return. If you think it's all about control, then this is a problem. People think that filmmaking is like multitask prompting, like AI. “Oh, I want this.” No, you're really building. It's a very, very dirty, non-linear business. And that's why one of the many reasons I'm against generative AI, is because it'll get you to mediocrity really quick. It'll get you to the middle really quick. And that may be an image. It's not film. It's not cinema.
Brian Altano (IGN): I think it's a very cynical approach to creating stuff where you only want the results and not the process. And the process is the fun part.
Guillermo del Toro: Let me put it this way: I can tell you, “Look, I'm faster than Usain Bolt.” I said, "Really?" I go, "Yeah, in my car." "Okay, well then, you're not a runner. You're in a car. It's not a f**king sport. That's not art. You're in a car."
Brian Altano (IGN): I think that's my favorite thing anyone has ever said about AI.
Guillermo del Toro: And you're in a f**king Volvo.
Brian Altano (IGN): Thank you so much for that. I'm very much against generative AI, and that is the best way it could possibly be put.
Guillermo del Toro: Look, the risk is this. Every single bad idea in the history of totalitarianism comes involved in a concept that sounds reasonably beneficial. The mother, the motherland — sounds really nice. Democratization of the arts. It's not that. They want your money. They want you to buy their app. They don't care about that. The discourse between the soul of mankind and the arts is a very sacred discourse. It's very intimate. It's molecularly important to stay human. Please, please. Don't give me an app. Please.
Brian Altano (IGN): I will not. Your unmade filmography is legendary.
Guillermo del Toro: Yes.
Brian Altano (IGN): Somewhere it exists in your brain. How do those sort of stories, those movies, live on? Do you ever go back through your sketchbooks? Can you watch them in your mind?
Guillermo del Toro: No. They're in the sketchbooks, and sometimes I repurpose ideas. For example, the wings of the Angel of Death came from a project that I was writing in ‘98. Partially, the Pale Man came from a sketch I did in ‘99. So you repurpose. Your diaries with drawings become a sort of catalog and you go through them and go, "Oh, I've never done that. Let me do it now." There's a sketch for a thing that I designed for Pan’s Labyrinth that is coming out in a stop motion movie I'm doing now.
Brian Altano (IGN): That’s awesome. I love that. So, you find a way to reincorporate these old ideas even if —
Guillermo del Toro: Well, it's a dialogue with yourself.
Brian Altano (IGN): Yeah.
Guillermo del Toro: You're talking to the time when you were a very different person. So you reactivate yourself.
Brian Altano (IGN): We talked about Pan's Labyrinth turning 20 this year. This was definitely the first movie that kind of broke over the crust of the usual people that were coming to your movies. All of a sudden, you had film critics and stuff like that [who] were really paying attention to you. Did that change you, having these new sets of eyes on you?
Guillermo del Toro: Well, Chronos and Devil's Backbone had that, but they had it in a very, very arthouse niche. What Pan's Labyrinth did is, the first movie that I willed to do my way with a slightly larger scale — The Shape of Water. And Pan’s Labyrinth cost exactly the same, $19.3 million, both movies. And [I looked] at the scale. And I said, "I'm going to will..." Alejandro González Iñárritu one day said to me, because I said, "How the hell did you do Birdman for that money?" And he said, "A budget is a state of mind." And you know what? It is. If you can find a way to scale the movie, you need a few things. For example, I was watching Pan’s Labyrinth when we were re-timing the color and I saw the huge locomotive, the rail locomotive, which is a real set. Now it took an inordinate amount of money to build that out of a budget that was very small to build that locomotive. But I said, "We need it. We need it for people to..." There are two or three or four gestures in Pan’s Labyrinth where people go, "Oh, it's a big movie." It's almost like you want to impress somebody and you pick up the check a couple of times. Not every time. Same with the movie. You have to pick up the check every so many minutes.
Brian Altano (IGN): I mean, I think the audience sees it and they connect with it. I think that people get that. I do believe that when audiences have this feeling that something is real, it washes over them, and they invest.
Guillermo del Toro: They absolutely do. I mean, look, I'm not going to go back to AI gratuitously. I will go for a point. Everything I've seen, the eyes are dead. It's like watching a flowerpot in the shape of a human. There's nothing inside. There's just air. How do you substitute a treasure as precious as an actor's eyes? You can't. With craftsmanship, if you see a set and you know it's made by humans, there's a nobility and there's a lineage and there's an elated feeling you get. “Oh, I didn't know that was possible.” It's so beautiful.
Brian Altano (IGN): You are a huge fan of video games, which I've always loved about you. I think that's so cool. And you sort of famously tried to get a couple of games going.
Guillermo del Toro: I'm the albatross of video games.
Brian Altano (IGN): You worked on P.T., you were working with Hideo Kojima.
Guillermo del Toro: It was a great game.
Brian Altano (IGN): Our audience, everyone and all my friends, we were ecstatic when we found out that you were working on a horror game with Kojima.
Guillermo del Toro: And that was Kojima. I mean, I'm glad to get on the ride for free, but everything that ended up being P.T., it was him.
Brian Altano (IGN): But around 11 years ago, I think at Comic-Con actually, you said you never wanted to work on a video game again.
Guillermo del Toro: No, never.
Brian Altano (IGN): Has that changed at all?
Guillermo del Toro: No, not at all.
Brian Altano (IGN): Wow.
Guillermo del Toro: It's simply too – we developed Insane, and then that went down. A lot of the ideas later, I saw stuff that was done in other video games that was similar. And I went, "Well, somebody did it. That's great." But we were aiming really high.
Brian Altano (IGN): Were you ever able to sort of, in the same way [with] your unmade movies, cherry pick some of those video game ideas and put them into your movies?
Guillermo del Toro: No, not on that. I mean, with Kojima, I had an idea that he didn't use that I hope to use in a different media someday. But with Hideo, the great thing is to go to karaoke and Shabu-shabu. If the game happens or not, it's immaterial. He knows very good restaurants.
Brian Altano (IGN): Dinner and karaoke is number one.
Guillermo del Toro: I love that man. He's one of those guys you meet that you go, you might as well be in the Renaissance. You are in front of a pure artist, and he cares about one thing: stories. That's it.
Brian Altano (IGN): I love that.
Guillermo del Toro: Jim Cameron, same thing. But with two guns and a belt of bullets. Jim is like, I've never met nor will I ever meet, nor mankind will ever have, somebody with a will like he has and the intelligence.
Brian Altano (IGN): You've created tons of original stories, but you've also played in other people's sandboxes sort of with adaptations, classic stuff like Pinocchio and Frankenstein. You don't want to make a video game ever. We'll close that door for good, but would you ever adapt a video game story into a movie?
Guillermo del Toro: You know, I tried. We had a very contentious call about a couple of games. I find that the dynamics of a video game are very different than a movie. They may be cinematically similar in terms of the camera moving and this and that, but the storytelling is very different, because you're not solving puzzles. You're not assembling. When we made the structure for Insane, we created what I call a mandala. You have to give the illusion of an infinite sandbox and you lead audiences to the right or to the left through their ‘own decisions,’ but you sort of have to corner them. So it's a very different thing. So adapting it, BioShock, we had a couple of calls. They are probably one of the most disastrous calls I've ever had. So no, f**k no.
Brian Altano (IGN): I want to talk to you a bit about creating your own world versus adapting someone else. Do you go into those things with the same philosophy, when you make an original story?
Guillermo del Toro: I have to.
Brian Altano (IGN): You have to.
Guillermo del Toro: You have to. I mean, my Pinocchio is not, and it is, Pinocchio. My Frankenstein is as referential, but as different as it needs to be to the text. You want the text by the book. You do the movie. Read it and make your own movie. That's easy. It's on the shelf. You're not altering it. You're not going and saying every book now has to reflect my movie. No. And the book exists, and it's so intimate. So what you do is a very interesting process. For example, what I do is I take the entire book and I drop it on final draft. Then I accumulate research material and I drop it on final draft. The Crimean War and Atomy Lessons, all of that. Then I lay all my books pertinent to that on a table. Then I do notes. And then finally, I ended up with Frankenstein, and it was like a 700-and-something-page working document, originally. And then you go line by line and you say, "I am out. I don't need it. I don't need this. I need this." You write on the side of a piece of paper. And little by little, you sort of get into the DNA of the story, and you wear it and you zip it up and then you take a walk. You say, "Okay, now I exist in this world. Where do I want to go today?" And then the rule is, “Am I interested or am I bored?” If you are bored when you're writing it, the audiences will be bored when they're watching it. But if you are intrigued, and then you say, "What are the fundamental questions the audience has about this material? What are the fundamental set pieces?" Pinocchio or Frankenstein both have to have a creation scene. You want to see them being put together. So you must. Pinocchio must join a carnival. He must declare what it is to be human. If it's the original thing, he has to become a boy. If it's in my story, he just has to be himself and sacrifice himself, and so on and so forth. And then you are wearing the world. When my kids were young, we would go and I would say, "Look, we're not going to have an agenda. When we're in Paris, we're not going to say 10 to 10:15, Eiffel Tower. 10:30 to 10:45, the Arc de Triomphe. No, because that's being a tourist.
Brian Altano (IGN): That's a terrible way to vacation.
Guillermo del Toro: I said, "We're travelers. Wherever we are, at any given time in the day, we're in Paris. That's it. So relax, breathe in, breathe out.” Same with this. Wherever we are, if we are wearing the world, you are in Frankenstein. You are in Pinocchio. People may have an issue. Why wouldn't I have done it like that? Good. Take 20 years of your life and show me your version."
Brian Altano (IGN): And you know what? I would rather see something like that and feel something than see an adaptation. And there's been so many, even recently of Pinocchio where you feel nothing.
Guillermo del Toro: It's about, does it evoke the latent potency of the myth? I mean, when I saw the Odyssey, did it make me feel that it was oomph filmmaking? Was I watching something that was monumental, epic, completely intended? Yes. Was it exactly what? I don't care. I'm there to see what he did. If you go and if you listen to the Sex Pistols singing my way, you don't talk about Frank Sinatra. You would be absolutely remiss to say, "Well, Sinatra did it different.” Of course he did it different, moron, it’s Sinatra. These are the fucking Sex Pistols. Listen to them. Don't listen to a thing that is not playing on the fucking radio.
Brian Altano (IGN): I love that. Yeah. I think that's the way it should be, right?
Guillermo del Toro: That's the way it is.
Brian Altano (IGN): It is the way it is. I think my beef with a lot of stuff now is that people want a literal one-to-one adaptation of a thing that they already experienced.
Guillermo del Toro: Well, I don't think it's even that. I mean, I think that we — There was a joke. It used to be about the French, the joke. Two Frenchmen are arguing on the street and a third one comes in and says, "I don't know what you're talking about, but I disagree." That's the internet. Two people arguing on something, and somebody has to come in and put both of them in their place.
Brian Altano (IGN): Yes.
Guillermo del Toro: There's no need. The universe is not binary. The universe is diverse. There are so many answers that suit so many people, that the fact that we want to enthrone black-and-white existence instead of a delightful myriad of great possibilities, which are suited to your moment, to your soul, it's dictatorial. I think that the level of human discourse after COVID got noticeably low. And I think now we came out of it a little crazier, a little meaner, and we cannot — there's the Zoolander Center for people that can't read good. That's where we are. We exist in the Zoolander Center for people that can't read good.
Brian Altano (IGN): I think, obviously, there's a little bit of hope I guess, on the optimistic side, is that this year there's been a really interesting resurgence or surgence, of younger filmmakers making original horror movies.
Guillermo del Toro: And a younger audience going to it. I mean, look, it is the horrible duty of the young to prove every f**king moron that came before them wrong. That's historically the duty of the young. That's why it's so hard to be young. I'm 62, I take anticoagulants. I'm past that. But it is the duty of the young to say, "We won't stand. This aggression will not stand, dude." They have to. And I think every now and then — I'm old enough that I was there when Blair Witch rephrased a certain way — I mean, I was there as a kid when George [Lucas] or Steven [Spielberg] came in with Jaws or Star Wars, and we've never seen anything like it. I was there when. So every now and then, things have to get rephrased. But storytelling is what makes us what we are humans. So it needs to be rephrased. You cannot hold the academia of it all only. There are two functions that are very different: The academic tradition exists not as a gatekeeper, but as a gate opener. Now, come on in and rearrange the room. That's the way I see or work. That's why I like the extras on the Blu-rays. It's not, “Look at how it's done.” No, it's like, “These are the tools. What are you going to do with them?”
Brian Altano (IGN): You can make it, too. So you're optimistic for the future?
Guillermo del Toro: I'm optimistic about the possibilities, yeah. Very much so. When you talk about the medieval [period], when people say, “The Middle Ages were very dark.” Well, in Europe, not in Mesoamerica, not in the North of Africa. There were cultures where they were flourishing. When I talk about movies and cinema, I don't just talk about American large-scale cinema. There are so many interesting movies in Europe, in Asia, and there's really interesting movies in Latin America. There's always great stories being told somewhere, so look for them. And the other day, the daughter of a friend of mine, she's listening to Karen Carpenter and her favorite song, We've Only Just Begun. I go, "What kind of maze do you have to go to be 12, 13, and like Karen Carpenter?" Well, the world and the library of the world is there to be rediscovered. Peter Bogdanovich used to say, "There are not old movies, just movies you have not seen." So when I discovered The Maltese Falcon for the first time, when I discovered Ikiru, the Kurosawa movie for the first time, it didn't matter when it was made. It was fresh for me.
Brian Altano (IGN): I think that's the perfect place to end. Thank you so much for your time, Mr. Del Toro. I hope you get to keep making cool monsters forever.
Guillermo del Toro: I hope I take a vacation. That's really what I want.
Brian Altano (IGN): Can we do a quick lightning round? And then I'll let you out of here.
Guillermo del Toro: Yeah, man.
Brian Altano (IGN): Okay, here we go. I'm going to have to keep you as quick as possible here.
Guillermo del Toro: Let’s do this.
Brian Altano (IGN): What is the first thing that ever scared you?
Guillermo del Toro: The Outer Limits, an episode called The Mutant. In terms of audiovisual scares. The first thing that scared me was my dad.
Brian Altano (IGN): What's the most recent thing that scared you?
Guillermo del Toro: Oh, the news.
Brian Altano (IGN): Same. What's the scariest movie ever made?
Guillermo del Toro: Well, it's personal. I mean, I think it really is. I would say for me, if I'm experiencing it in the theater, Alien and The Shining and Jaws. Those three had me on the edge of my seat.
Brian Altano (IGN): What's your favorite movie monster of all time?
Guillermo del Toro: That's hard, but the creature of Frankenstein or the Creature from the Black Lagoon, it's a toss up.
Brian Altano (IGN): What's the best video game ever made?
Guillermo del Toro: They're so different. I mean, I love Left 4 Dead. Death Stranding made me cry. Shadow of the Colossus made me introspective about so many intangible things. There's not only one. BioShock! It's a world I could get lost in for ages.
Brian Altano (IGN): What's the most recent great video game that you've played?
Guillermo del Toro: I'm more into, not necessarily console games. Dead Cells was really interesting to me. I just hate respawning because you get all the way there, you go all the way to 35 levels, and then you start again, and you get faster! But please, please do a version without respawning. For the older, elderly players, please give us a way to come back.
Brian Altano (IGN): Life is short. I don't want to keep responding.
Guillermo del Toro: I'm available. Contact me and send it to me, please. I beg you. I like the world. Great design.
Brian Altano (IGN): I think you'd like Castlevania. That's kind of -
Guillermo del Toro: Yeah, I've never played Castlevania.
Brian Altano (IGN): That's what you're looking for. It's Dead Cells, but you don’t have to start from the beginning every time.
Guillermo del Toro: Really? Well, there's a lot of games I have not played. So if you can recommend, yeah.
Brian Altano (IGN): I'll get you a list.
Guillermo del Toro: Journey.
Brian Altano (IGN): Journey's amazing.
Guillermo del Toro: Amazing. Oh my God, what a bite. Monument Valley.
Brian Altano (IGN): Yes.
Guillermo del Toro: These are worlds that I love. And then every day of my life, every moment I have free, I'm still playing Angry Birds.
Brian Altano (IGN): Angry Birds?
Guillermo del Toro: I'm really good at it. I'm really good at it.
Brian Altano (IGN): Guillermo, you could have given me a thousand guesses, and I would not have pinned you as an Angry Birds guy.
Guillermo del Toro: It's not exactly a connoisseur choice, but every day, every day is ridiculous. It's like I just go, let me hit this. I want all the stars, a perfect game on every level they ever put out.
Brian Altano (IGN): I love it. I love it. Thank you so much for your time today. This is a blast. My
Guillermo del Toro: My pleasure. Thank you. Best of luck.
Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze.

item.title: A prominent Call of Duty esports commentator has opted to resign from his role after pursuing a romantic relationship with his co-commentator's ex-wife.
item.description:
A prominent Call of Duty esports commentator has opted to resign from his role after pursuing a romantic relationship with his co-commentator's ex-wife.
In what is one of the most unique stories of the week, Call of Duty League commentator Clint "Maven" Evans has announced that he's stepping away from the CDL for the "foreseeable future." He noted that this decision came after he chose to pursue a romantic relationship with the wife of his co-commentator, Joseph "MerK" DeLuca. Evans noted that he recognized that the situation is "taboo" and "unconventional" in a statement.
"As some of you know, I was very close to my casting partner Joe and his family," Evans wrote. "Maurisa was one of my best friends. We remained friends, after they divorced, and along the way it became more than that and we started dating. I understand how unconventional/taboo it is. It’s truly not something I ever foresaw happening."
He went on to note that he hopes to return to the CDL in the future, but has acknowledged that it may not happen.
"I hope that one day I’ll be back working on the CDL," he continued. "If not, it was a hell of a ride, and I appreciate the love over the years. Please continue to show support to Joe, the CDL, and its talent!"
Naturally, the Call of Duty e-sports community has had some very intense reactions to the news. Many feel that Evans betrayed his friend, whom he has known for well over a decade. DeLuca hasn't commented on the situation and hasn't posted on his X page since October 4. The start date for the upcoming CDL season has yet to be formally announced, but historically, it begins in December, shortly after the latest Call of Duty is released.
Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

item.title: Gears of War: E-Day launched this week, and while it is excellent, the game was pulled away from a PS5 launch earlier this year. But, in a recent interview, The Coalition Studio Head Mike Crump claims that it is all part of the plan.
item.description:
Gears of War: E-Day launched this week, and while it is excellent, the game was pulled away from a PS5 launch earlier this year. In a recent interview, The Coalition Studio Head Mike Crump claims that this was all part of the plan.
In an interview with the BBC, Crump defended the choice to be an Xbox exclusive, despite a likely ludicrous budget saying, "Gears has been an exclusive franchise to Xbox for 20 years now. It's sort of entwined deeply with the brand."
However, Gears of War: Reloaded did launch on PS5 last year, so the franchise as a whole isn't exactly Xbox-exclusive anymore. It's also likely that if E-Day did launch on PlayStation, it'd see higher sales numbers.
Crump claims that the metrics for success go further than that, though. He told the BBC that the series is meant to, at least in part, carry the banner for the Xbox platform and give people a "reason to be in the Xbox ecosystem." Queue Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's decision to pull the game from the PS5 release slate.
Regardless, the game will now likely have lower sales than it otherwise would have. When the BBC asked Crump about that, he insisted that the studio is taking a broader view than just looking at sales figures and retention numbers.
"We measure things like, are we showcasing the platform? Are we pushing the hardware to it limits? Are we showcasing what the Xbox is capable of? ...Our goal basically is to be the best-looking game on the Xbox and really show the industry what's possible with our hardware," he answered.
If the goal is to be a tech demo about what the Xbox consoles are capable of, I'd argue that it's a straight-up success. The game looks incredible on both the Xbox Series X and Series S, so much so that The Coalition had to rely on trickery with the Page File to get the game running smoothly on the less-powerful console. The game is also incredible, and our reviewer Ryan McCaffrey gave it a 9, saying:
"By going back to the beginning, Gears of War: E-Day returns to the heart of this series: Marcus Fenix, Dom Santiago, and a Locust horde that’s as terrifying as it is dangerous. E-Day pulls off the tightrope act of giving us a heartfelt prequel with strong characters even when we know how it ends. On a more mechanical level, it also evolves the enemies, weapons, and combat you’d expect to deliver a Gears of War campaign that stands toe-to-toe with any of the others. It wraps up with 10 years still left to go before Marcus gets tossed in prison ahead of the events of the first Gears of War, so here’s hoping the next one stays in the past for a while longer – and that we don’t have to wait another seven years for it to arrive."
But even if the game is a critical hit and a technical marvel, sales numbers will inevitably play a role in the game's success, especially as Microsoft is currently in the middle of a months-long restructuring campaign. Right after launch, developers at The Coalition told Eurogamer they were expecting layoffs. However, Crump has since addressed those concerns, saying, "For us that's about shipping a great game that people are going to love and I feel like, as a team, we've done that."
Let's just hope that a pretty game and high review scores really are enough to keep the Xbox layoff machine at bay.

item.title: Resident Evil and Street Fighter developer Capcom has clarified its stance on AI and its future plans for the RE Engine in an exclusive conversation with IGN.
item.description:
Resident Evil and Street Fighter developer Capcom has clarified its stance on AI and its future plans for the RE Engine in an exclusive conversation with IGN.
Capcom held its yearly recruitment conference on October 2, wherein programmer Satoshi Ishida outlined the company’s plans to incrementally improve its RE Engine using a program called REX (short for RE Next Engine).
Rather than building a new engine from scrap, Ishida explained that a series of steps will be taken to improve the RE Engine piece by piece. This includes the use of AI, which gave fans pause after the news broke online.
We bent the ear of a spokesperson at Capcom, who laid out the challenges its developers are currently facing that led the company to rethink how it makes games with the RE Engine. They confirmed that games are becoming increasingly colossal undertakings, to the point where titles now take up immense amounts of time and resources to create. With AI being a swiftly advancing technology, Capcom saw the opportunity to use it to solve these issues and make its developers more efficient by improving their development tools, testing game code for them, and analyzing large chunks of data on their behalf, as well as other helpful benefits.
Capcom’s vision for REX is to implement these AI tools and efficiencies into the next iteration of the RE Engine to help the company make games faster with the strongest tools available to it. The spokesperson told us that Capcom has no plans to use generative AI in the creation of its games (which creates content based on a prompt, as opposed to other types of AI that are used to analyze patterns, make predictions, process data, etc.). Any AI used with the RE Engine will be for the express purpose of speeding up processes and helping development teams be more efficient.
This means that AI will not be used for creating assets or programs in games. Capcom said as much back in March during a shareholders’ meeting, where the company was asked how it intends to use artificial intelligence in its products.
“We will not implement assets generated by AI into our games.” Capcom said. “However, we plan to proactively use it as a contributing technology to improve the efficiency and productivity of the game development process. To this end, we are currently exploring ways to implement it in various areas, including graphics, sound and programming."
Upcoming Capcom games include Resident Evil Veronica and Mega Man: Dual Override.

item.title: The FBI arrested a Fortnite player last week after Epic reported threats he made over voice chat.
item.description:
The FBI arrested a Fortnite player last week after Epic reported threats he made over voice chat.
Epic reported Edward Frith, an avid Fortnite player from Alabama, over alarming messages spoken while playing Fortnite. He was later arrested when the FBI turned up at his house.
According to the affidavit (reported by Aftermath), Frith, who went by the username “WagesOfNinja,” said he was letting all his rage out because he wanted to “literally murder somebody” and that he thinks about killing “every day.”
"Let's see if the FBI is going to show up at my door because I'll shoot them motherf****rs too," Frith said, before the FBI showed up at his door. Frith’s other comments were just as disturbing, with the Fortnite player suggesting he was planning to end his life by charging at police.
Epic made what was described as a "voluntary emergency disclosure" to the FBI National Threat Operations Section (NTOS) Exigent Threat Research and Analysis Crisis Team (EXTRACT), relating to the statements. The developer then provided the FBI with an audio recording and transcript of the threats.
The Alabama resident was indicted for violating Interstate Threatening Communications on September 23. He was remanded into custody while awaiting a trial, after entering a plea of “not guilty” on September 24.
Epic Games announced a new voice reporting system for Fortnite in November 2023. The system allows players to clip audio and anonymously file a report whenever they catch another player violating the community rules.
"The only way Epic ever receives a copy of the audio clip is if voice reporting is on and a participant affirmatively reports the voice chat using the in-game voice reporting feature,” Epic said at the time.
Once reported, the last five minutes of communications are captured and the audio file is sent to Epic’s moderation team to review. Depending on the severity of the communications, players can face bans or, in this case, being reported to the feds.
Likewise, Fortnite players can report text chat, which is stored for 30 days. The Fortnite developer also uses autonomous systems to detect harmful language, such as “self-harm, child endangerment, and threats of real-world violence.”

item.title: Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is set to return to IMAX as Digger's run comes to an end a week after launch.
item.description:
Tom Cruise’s latest movie, Digger, made around $20 million worldwide on its opening weekend. The film, which buries Cruise under thick makeup to make the ageless star look like a normal old man, reportedly had a $160 million production budget (via Deadline). I’m no math genius, but is that good?
Meanwhile, Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey currently sits at $1.76 billion from theatres after what has been a spectacular run at the box office. Again, I’m not a math guy, but that’s a fair bit more.
Digger, which was shot in VistaVision, was released on IMAX screens on October 2, but its time on the bigger big screen is almost at an end already. The Odyssey will return to select IMAX theaters this Friday, October 9, replacing the Cruise flick.
With only 41 theatres worldwide equipped to play true IMAX, fitted with the specialized 15-perf/70mm film projectors capable of displaying the movie in its ideal ratio, it’s understandable. Especially if those cinemas want to make any money.
The next films with planned IMAX releases are Street Fighter on October 16, and Godzilla Minus Zero starting on November 3. Until then, there’s a small window of opportunity to see The Odyssey as Nolan intended.
IGN’s review of Digger called the script its "Achilles heel.” It has a 51% rating on Rotten Tomatoes' Tomatometer. Digger trolled the negative reviews in its most recent ad campaign, but that failed to move the needle.
The Odyssey was, of course, well-received, but it didn’t please everyone. Emily Wilson, the translator whose work inspired Nolan's adaptation of Homer's poem, hated it so much that she’s retranslating The Iliad in its entirety.
The Odyssey is currently the second highest-grossing movie of the year, behind only Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which has now passed well over $2 billion at the box office.

item.title: The boss of Gears of War: E-Day developer The Coalition has responded to reports that staff at the studio are worried they will lose their jobs amid the ongoing cuts at Xbox, and promised the next Gears game won’t take as long to make.
item.description:
The boss of Gears of War: E-Day developer The Coalition has responded to reports that staff at the studio are worried they will lose their jobs amid the ongoing cuts at Xbox, and promised the next Gears game won’t take as long to make.
Earlier this month, Eurogamer reported on serious internal concern that layoffs would hit The Coalition after the release of E-Day. "The mood is certainly 'let's not celebrate the game until we're three months post launch, just in case,' which is very unusual," one source told the site. "We're just expecting the next wave [of layoffs], or being reorganized under Activision or something later this year," claimed another.
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma’s “reset” of Microsoft’s gaming business has seen nearly 2,000 people cut already this financial year, with more to come. A number of studios have left the business or are in the process of closing down. Microsoft has also reorganized its studios, bringing Halo and Sea of Thieves developer Rare under Call of Duty developer Activision, and Grounded developer Obsidian under Fallout developer Bethesda.
The Coalition has, for the most part, avoided the cuts, although E-Day's story director was laid off just one week before the game's early access launch. The BBC put Eurogamer’s report to The Coalition studio head Mike Crump, who danced around the issue in his response.
"What I say to myself, what I say to the team, is we need to focus on the things that we can control,” Crump said.
"For us that's about shipping a great game that people are going to love and I feel like, as a team, we've done that."
No guarantee, then, that The Coalition will escape the fate suffered by so many at Xbox this summer. But Crump did suggest there are plans for more Gears of War games. He called E-Day a "great foundation" for future games in the series, and said "the next game will not take nearly as long" to make.
As for what the next Gears game is, in June 2024, Microsoft pledged to continue the story of Gears of War and wrap up the cliffhanger posed by Gears 5's ending, despite creating a prequel first with E-Day. The question is, will The Coalition get the chance to make it?

item.title: Mafia 2 and Mafia 3 are coming to PS5 and Xbox Series consoles with some prettier graphics, according to an ESRB rating.
item.description:
Mafia 2 and Mafia 3 are coming to PS5 and Xbox Series consoles with some prettier graphics, according to an ESRB rating. Both games are rated Mature 17+ by the board, with each title featuring violence, nudity, and so… many… slurs.
Previously, Mafia: Definitive Edition released for modern consoles in September 2020. A full-blown, ground-up remake of the original 2002 game, it acted as a great starting point for people jumping into the series for the first time. Mafia 2 and 3 Definitive Editions already exist for the last-gen consoles, so these listings presumably relate to current-gen upgrades that will, hopefully, include 60fps gameplay, rather than full-blown remakes.
Publisher 2K recently released the Mafia: The Omertà Collection, which includes all the Definitive Editions alongside Mafia: The Old Country Definitive Edition. This launched alongside a PS5 and Xbox Series update to Mafia: Definitive Edition that seems likely to be replicated for Mafia 2 and 3.
Interest in the series is at a new high following the release of Mafia: The Old Country earlier this year. A prequel story set at the height of the mob’s power in Italy, it followed the series’ template of plonking players into an open world that serves as a backdrop to the story, rather than a character in it.
IGN’s Mafia: The Old Country review scored it an 8/10, and called the game an “effective return to the linear and tightly story-driven format of the original Mafia and Mafia 2.” Mafia 3 split critics at launch because it leaned into its open world and made players complete repeatable missions to capture territory and progress the story. Amazing soundtrack, though.
Hangar 13 president Nick Baynes previously told IGN that Mafia and GTA — despite sharing a parent company — exist in two separate camps. “I think that genuinely at the studio, we've got our own path,” Baynes said. “It genuinely never ever comes up in conversation as a touchpoint or steering our strategy or anything like that.”
The ESRB posting doesn’t give much away, besides rehashing themes you’d expect from a game series named after an organized crime group. It’ll be interesting to see which side of GTA 6’s release date this November these Definitive Editions end up. Because while the games are fairly different, the audience only has limited disposable income and that choice has probably already been made if the games land anywhere near each other.
IGN just put out a big GTA 6 interview with Rockstar North studio head Rob Nelson, in which we spoke to him as he played a section of the game in front of us. Nelson spoke about its approach to open world design, and creating a game where “just existing” is a viable playstyle, living in Vice City and playing it almost like a life simulator.
It’s a very different approach to Mafia, in which the open world is simply a backdrop to the story. Still, isn’t it great that we live in a world where both approaches are viable and we get to experience it all?
A Mafia 2 and Mafia 3: Definitive Edition announcement is likely imminent, either way. My best guess would be The Game Awards this December, with a launch early next year. While you wait to find out, check out IGN's in-depth feature, 25 Years of Mafia Video Games: An Oral History.

item.title: According to a report from French site Dealabs, Forza Horizon 6 will finally land on PS5 early next year.
item.description:
According to a report from reliable leaker billbil-kun on French site Dealabs, Forza Horizon 6 will finally land on PS5 early next year, despite Microsoft insisting it would make it out by the end of 2026.
Playground's well-received racer launched on Xbox Series X and S and PC in May 2026. The PS5 version is now set to dodge a collision with GTA 6, which seems to have its own track and street racing, and will reportedly release on January 26, 2027.
In August, Tom Warren from The Verge said that Forza Horizon 6 wouldn't hit PS5 this year. At the time, Playground released a statement insisting Forza Horizon 6 would. Playground has yet to issue a fresh comment following today's report.
Since Xbox CEO Asha Sharma took over from the retired Phil Spencer earlier this year, Microsoft's gaming strategy has shifted to encompass limited Xbox console exclusives. Gears of War: E-Day, for example, will not release on PS5. Neither will inXile's Clockwork Revolution, which was made an Xbox console exclusive.
Forza Horizon 6, however, has avoided a similar fate. Perhaps that's no surprise, given Forza Horizon 5 reportedly sold over 5 million copies on PS5, generating more than $300 million in revenue. Surely Forza Horizon 6 will generate signifcant revenue on PS5 also.
IGN’s Forza Horizon 6 review returned a 10/10. We called it “the best-looking and best-sounding game Playground has produced to date, set in the most wonderfully realised map it’s ever crafted.”
According to billbil-kun, a PS5 physical edition will land at the same time as the digital version. Earlier this year, Sony announced plans to phase out discs on PlayStation by 2028, sparking massive pushback and petitions with hundreds of thousands of signatories.
The report claims the price for Forza Horizon 6 on PS5 will align with the Xbox version, meaning it’ll cost around $69.99. As a first-party game, it's also available as part of Game Pass, although there are question marks over Microsoft's subscription strategy and day one releases. In July, the former director of Forza Horizon traced a line from the failure of the "well-meaning" Game Pass to the current layoffs sweeping across Xbox.
Just this week, Playground issued a statement finally addressing its community after months of constructive feedback about Forza Horizon 6 was met with nothing but radio silence from the renowned British studio. A second team at Playground is also in the final stretch of development on the Fable reboot, which is due to be released on Xbox, PC, and PS5 on February 23, 2027.
Kirk McKeand is a Contributor on IGN News. Find him on Twitter @MckKirk

item.title: The AI video game clone explosion continues at pace. Now, someone has made Minecraft playable inside X / Twitter with working multiplayer.
item.description:
The AI video game clone explosion continues at pace. Now, someone has made Minecraft playable inside X / Twitter with working multiplayer. X user jaivin used AI to make Mojang’s Minecraft playable inside posts on Elon Musk’s social network, and is letting people buy in-game sponsorships with cryptocurrency.
“Tweetcraft is a block game in a post: every world is a link on X, and everyone who opens it plays together,” reads the official blurb. “Put your ad at the top of the server list, in a world’s sponsor leaderboard, or your logo on the Block Dragon.”
So, what’s going on here? Essentially, "Tweetcraft" is a custom browser-based Minecraft clone where you generate a shared world and post its unique link on X / Twitter, which acts as a shared entry point. Anyone who clicks on the link joins the same real-time multiplayer session. The game itself renders in your browser.
This “port” is, obviously, unauthorized, and will no doubt draw the attention of Microsoft’s lawyers sooner rather than later. Jaivin’s launch post has had 7.4 million views already. Various follow-up posts detail an explosion of popularity as people try it out.
Perhaps in a bid to downplay any potential trademark or copyright infringement, jaivin has called the game “Tweetcraft,” although it’s clearly Minecraft in shape and form. Jaivin also insisted that “Tweetcraft uses none of Minecraft's assets and is not associated with Mojang or Microsoft.”
Responses are similar to those we’ve seen over the last two weeks amid this AI-powered video game clone and “game-merging” mod explosion, which has spawned a number of viral gameplay clips of famous video game franchises mashed together. There’s a mix of excitement and disgust, with some saying a clampdown is inevitable.
“The name is brilliant because now you can lose two separate trademark lawsuits,” one person said of Tweetcraft.
“The ‘I do not own this music video’ description when uploading a music video on YouTube defense,” another said.
October has already seen GTA 5 and the original version of Halo on Xbox made playable on a browser, with more surely to come. The GTA 5 clone was hit by a takedown, as was a Fallout: New York game that was released in-browser.
Clearly, this Whack-a-Mole between IP owner and AI-generated video game isn’t sustainable, so the question will be what the video game industry does long term to prevent this sort of thing happening in the first place. Indeed, can it do anything? With AI models becoming increasingly powerful, the time it takes for unauthorized versions of established video games to appear outside of official platforms will reduce potentially to just hours or even minutes. With GTA 6 releasing on PS5 and Xbox Series X and S only, how long will it take for someone to use AI to make it playable on PC via a browser?

item.title: A new Ape Escape video game is reportedly in the works, helmed by the team that successfully rebooted a certain blue hedgehog with Sonic Mania.
item.description:
A new Ape Escape video game is reportedly in the works, helmed by the team that successfully rebooted a certain blue hedgehog with Sonic Mania. Developer Evening Star also made Penny’s Big Breakaway, which launched to mixed reviews compared to Sonic Mania’s near unanimous praise.
The report comes from journalist Jeff Gerstmann, corroborated by VGC sources. “So yeah, some other folks have said that they also heard that Ape Escape is being made,” Gerstmann said on his podcast.
“I don’t think this game is close to being out or anything like that, but I guess it’s been almost a year since we started talking about Ape Escape. “Who is making it? That’s a good question.
“My understanding is that it’s an external studio. People were immediately like, ‘Oh, Team Asobi (Astro Bot) is making it.’ My understanding is that an external team has been working on that. What do they make… Penny’s Big Breakaway. Evening Star. I heard that they were working on it.”
According to the report, Sony is looking at using third-party studios to revive dormant series across its entire portfolio. Last month, rumors were circulating that PlayStation is looking to bring back Killzone, though the obvious choice of developer for that one would likely be first-party original studio Guerrilla Games.
The last game in the Ape Escape series is PlayStation Move Ape Escape, released for PS3 in 2010. The last mainline game was Ape Escape 3, five years earlier, for PS2.
“At the time that I initially heard it, it sounded like it was a game that had been just barely greenlit and just getting underway," Gerstmann continued.
“You know, not necessarily the most corroborated, multiple-source thing, but that is what I heard about an Ape Escape Game. I was asking people questions at DICE this year about this Ape Escape game. So that was February. So there ya go.”
IGN reached out to Sony for comment about its rumored third-party licensing strategy last week, but so far there’s been no response.
